objective.statement: Find and name the cadences in a short musical passage.
successCriteria: I locate the two chords of a cadence point.
I name each chord and then the cadence.
I do not name a cadence from the melody alone.

explanation.text: In a real piece a cadence is made by several things together: the rhythm, the rise and fall of the melody, and the chords. At Grade 5 the cadence points are marked for you, and what is tested is whether you can tell from the chords what kind of cadence it is.

Look at the two chords at the marked place. Name each one by its root and position, then check them against the three patterns: V–I, IV–I, or a pair ending on V. A phrase can have more than one cadence point: a first cadence in the middle, and a last cadence at the end.

music.textAlternative: A phrase in C major with four chords, one in each bar: I, V, IV, I. The first cadence point is bars 1 to 2 (I–V). The last is bars 3 to 4 (IV–I).

explanation.caption: I–V (imperfect) at the first cadence point, IV–I (plagal) at the last.

explanation.text: A cadence is the harmony: do not name it from the melody or the rhythm alone. The same melody could be harmonised in more than one way, and some questions accept more than one pair of chords. The question always tells you where the cadence is.
Name the chords first. Then compare with V–I, IV–I and endings on V.

music.textAlternative: A phrase ending in D major: I then V.

steps: Chords: D F♯ A is I; A C♯ E is V.
I followed by V ends on the dominant.
demonstration.textAlternative: I–V in D major: an imperfect cadence.
